title: Steak au Poivre
subtitle: Pan-fried steak in a black pepper and brandy cream sauce
excerpt: Sirloin or rump steak coated in cracked black peppercorns and cooked in a very hot pan, then finished with a quick sauce of brandy, cream, and the pan juices. Ready in 15 minutes and one of the great bistro dishes.
sourceNotes: Steak au poivre became famous in the Parisian brasseries of the mid-20th century and is now one of the defining dishes of French bistro cooking. Auguste Escoffier, Le Guide Culinaire (1903), gives steak with peppercorns. The version with a brandy and cream pan sauce was popularised in the post-war Paris brasserie scene. Julia Child, Mastering the Art of French Cooking Vol. 2 (1970), gives a detailed method.

glossaryTerms.definition: The technique of pouring alcohol into a hot pan and igniting it briefly. The flame burns off the raw alcohol and leaves the flavour of the spirit. In steak au poivre, brandy is flambéed to give the sauce its distinctive depth without the harsh raw spirit taste. Tilt the pan away from you and use a long match or lighter.

content.text: Steak au poivre is a restaurant dish that can be made at home in 15 minutes. The pepper crust must be cracked coarsely, not ground fine, and pressed firmly into both sides of the steak before it goes into the very hot pan. The sauce is built in the same pan from the brandy (which is briefly
), the cream, and the pan juices from the steak. Serve immediately.

items.prepNote: whole peppercorns, coarsely cracked in a mortar or under a pan

content.text: Pat the steaks dry. Press the cracked pepper firmly into both sides of each steak with the flat of your hand. The pepper should form a visible crust, not a light dusting. Season the sides of the steak with salt but not the peppered faces, the pepper provides the seasoning.

Heat the cast-iron skillet until very hot, a drop of water should evaporate immediately. Add the oil and butter. When the butter foam subsides, add the steaks. Cook for 3 minutes without moving for medium-rare (60°C internal). Turn and cook 2 to 3 minutes more. Remove and rest on a warm plate loosely covered with foil for 5 minutes.

With the pan still on the heat, pour in the brandy carefully. Stand back and tilt the pan slightly, the brandy will ignite if using a gas flame. Allow to flame for 5 seconds, then swirl to extinguish. (If using induction, ignite with a long match.) The flame burns off the raw alcohol.

Add the cream and any resting juices from the steak. Stir to deglaze the pan, scraping up all the pepper and meat deposits. Simmer for 2 to 3 minutes until the sauce thickens enough to coat a spoon. Stir in the Dijon mustard if using. Taste and season.
Serve the steaks immediately with the sauce poured over or alongside. Pommes frites or a simple green salad alongside.

items.symptom: The pepper crust fell off during cooking
items.cause: The pepper was not pressed firmly enough, or the pan was not hot enough when the steak went in.
items.fix: Press the pepper hard into the steak and allow the crust to adhere for a few minutes before cooking. The pan must be at maximum heat, the steak should sizzle loudly on contact and immediately stick, then release when the crust has formed.

items.cause: The internal temperature exceeded the target before resting.
items.fix: For a 2.5 cm sirloin, 3 minutes each side at very high heat should give medium-rare. Use an instant-read thermometer: remove at 57°C, as carry-over during resting will take it to 60°C.

items.cause: The cream was added to a pan that was too hot.
items.fix: Remove from the heat for 30 seconds after flambéing before adding the cream. The cream should simmer, not boil violently, in the pan juices.

content.text: Steak au poivre is a Paris brasserie dish. The brasserie is a particular French institution: it serves food at all hours to a mixed crowd of businesspeople, tourists, and theatre-goers. The brandy-and-cream version of the sauce was established in the large brasseries of the grands boulevards in the 1950s and 1960s. It has been one of the most ordered dishes in French restaurants ever since. It is also a useful recipe for showing how a simple pan sauce can be made in the time it takes a steak to rest.
